title: The Interface Does Not Make Clear What an Action Will Affect
excerpt: This failure occurs when a user performs the intended action, but the interface applies it to a different object. The mechanism is a collapsed selected state that makes inspection and action target look like one variable.
metaTitle: When an Interface Hides an Action Target
metaDescription: A failure pattern where a correct action reaches the wrong object because inspection and target selection are not separated.
summary: This page defines the failure in which an interface does what the user asked, but to an object other than the one the user meant. It distinguishes that failure from discrimination errors, timing errors, state-visibility failures and post-action error detection.
definition: A wrong-object action failure occurs when the user performs the intended action deliberately, but the interface applies it to a different object because the object under inspection and the object an action will affect are collapsed into a single selected state.

bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

This failure occurs when a user performs the correct action, but the interface applies it to the wrong object. The task may be understood. The click or command may be deliberate. The error is that the action target is not the object the user had in mind.

The pattern includes category examples such as wrong-patient errors in clinical systems, wrong-account transfers in financial interfaces, wrong-machine commands on a factory floor and wrong-row deletion in administrative tools. Those examples describe the class of failure. They are not claims that Creative Navy designed clinical or financial systems for this page, and no incident is claimed to have occurred or been averted.

## Failure pattern: correct action, wrong object

A wrong-object action failure is a binding problem. The user may be looking at the right object and may choose the intended action, but the interface binds that action to a different object.

This differs from a discrimination problem. In a discrimination problem, the user cannot tell which of several similar elements is the right one before acting. In a binding problem, the user has identified the object under inspection, but the interface has not kept that object separate from the object an action will affect.

The design consequence is different. A discrimination problem is addressed by making the relevant element distinguishable from irrelevant elements. A binding problem is addressed by separating inspection from target selection, so the user can see both variables and change the action target deliberately.

## Selection components can collapse inspection and action target

Selection components commonly use one highlighted state to represent several meanings at once. A row, card or map object may look selected because the user is inspecting it, because it is the target of the next action, or because the system is implying that an operation is available for it.

When those meanings are collapsed, the interface can make a correct action reach a wrong object. The user may move from one object to another for inspection, but the system may silently retarget the next command. Or a pending transaction may remain bound to the original object while the visible inspection focus has moved elsewhere.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treats this as a behavioural specification problem, not only as a visual legibility problem. The interface must specify which variable is changing, what action changes it, and whether changing it sends any command outside the interface.

## Schone Airspace Group separated inspection from command target

Schone Airspace Group provides the anchor case for this failure pattern. In the Schone Airspace Group design, the inspected aircraft and the command target were independent variables with distinct visual treatments. The command target used a double solid outline and labelled badge. The inspected aircraft used a dotted outline and separate badge. Both could appear at once on the same card.

That design rejected a single generic selected state. The accepted cost was that two highlighted identities could be visible simultaneously, adding interface complexity in exchange for safer separation of operator intent.

Changing the command target required a named, explicit operator action. That action changed the recipient and sent no aircraft command. The engagement described this as deliberate friction: one additional explicit action was required to operate a different aircraft.

The Schone Airspace Group material also separated interface target selection from flight-controller authority. A selected interface target did not confer command authority. Eligibility and command-channel permission were independent checks resolved outside the interface, and the distinction required an additional status label.

A pending transaction also kept the aircraft it was dispatched against. If the operator inspected or targeted a different aircraft while a request was pending, the pending request kept its original recipient, action and request identifier. The new target did not rewrite that transaction history.

The Schone Airspace Group evidence is design-representation evidence. Scripted acceptance checks were run twice: first by Creative Navy, then by five of the nine operators who took part in the research. Each check fixed a starting state, an operator action and an expected visible response. A pass meant the interface stated the correct operational fact under that condition. The checks were not a measure of flight performance, operator proficiency, task completion time or error rate, and they were not conducted on a connected system.

Severity in the Schone Airspace Group evidence records the consequence of interface ambiguity within a scripted task. It does not state that a corresponding aircraft incident occurred.

## Raymarine shows what confirmation can and cannot do

Raymarine provides the strongest numeric evidence on this page. The comparison used two concepts with identical hardware mappings, identical AIS information and identical physical controls. The only variable was where the extra interaction was placed after the operator pressed the call action.

Wrong-recipient submissions were two of eight under immediate calling and zero of eight with confirmation. Initial wrong target selections still occurred: four of eight under immediate calling and three of eight under confirmation. Under the confirmation condition, all three initial errors were detected and corrected at the confirmation screen before any request was sent.

The cost was recorded in the same comparison. Median completion time was 17.95 seconds for immediate calling and 23.80 seconds for confirmed calling, a 5.85 second cost. Median physical actions were 6.0 immediate and 8.5 confirmed. That cost was accepted in the design decision.

The Raymarine evidence does not show that confirmation prevents target selection mistakes. It shows that confirmation made the recipient identity legible at a second decision point, giving operators the opportunity to detect and correct errors before a request was submitted.

The Raymarine evidence is limited to a bench prototype under a fixed scenario fixture with eight participants in the relevant comparison. The engagement tested nothing at a helm. Raymarine's own brief named wet hands and gloves, glare and night sailing, vibration, ambient noise and divided attention, and none of those conditions was tested.

## Oceaneering shows the same failure when the wrong object is a class

Oceaneering provides the everyday, high-frequency version of the same failure. In that engagement, the wrong object was not a specific instance such as one aircraft or one vessel. It was a selected cart type.

The hospital logistics context involved supply flatbeds being dispatched wrongly every day because people were in a hurry. The consequence was that the vehicle arrived, tried to lift, detected the wrong cart type, set the cart down and left without explaining why. The mismatch was detected after lifting, downstream of an operator who had usually walked away.

Creative Navy's design response in the Oceaneering dispatch panel let the next person at the depot tap the station holding the refused cart, read what the vehicle detected against what had been selected, confirm the detected type in one action, and re-enter destination and identity.

The Oceaneering evidence is not usability testing. The two sessions were design reviews, not tests; nothing was measured; and no dispatch operator took part. The case supports the mechanism and design response, not a measured performance or error-rate claim.

## Confirmation is a second decision point, not a prevention guarantee

Confirmation belongs on this page when it makes the action target visible at the moment of commitment. A confirmation step can expose the recipient, object, class or destination before the request is submitted.

Confirmation does not by itself make the first selection correct. The Raymarine comparison is the clearest example: initial wrong target selections still occurred under confirmation, but the confirmation screen gave operators a second point at which to detect and correct them.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method therefore treats confirmation as one possible form of friction, not as a universal fix. The design question is whether the extra step makes the target identity legible at the point where the user can still change the decision, and whether the cost of the extra step is acceptable for the task.

## Boundaries with adjacent failure pages

This page covers action-target ambiguity at the moment of commitment. It should not absorb every case where a user chooses the wrong element or makes an error.

Errors Are Easy To Make covers discrimination cases where interface complexity masks which element or condition is operative. In those cases, the user cannot tell which similar element is the right one before acting. This page covers the narrower case where the element has been identified correctly and the action still reaches another object.

Critical Actions Appear At The Wrong Time covers timing failures. There, an action that is correct in itself is surfaced at the wrong moment.

Users Cannot See What State The System Is In covers system-state visibility. That page concerns the state of the system, rather than the target object that an action will affect.

Errors Are Hard To Notice covers what happens after an error has occurred. This page concerns the moment of commitment, before or during the action that binds a request to a target.

The positive design principle is command integrity: the interface should make clear what command is being formed, what object it will affect, and which action changes that binding. This page documents the failure pattern rather than the full principle.

## Evidence basis and limits

The evidence base combines three engagements with different weights. Schone Airspace Group provides the main design mechanism and acceptance-check evidence for separating inspection and command target. Raymarine provides the strongest numeric comparison, with the result and cost of a confirmation step recorded together. Oceaneering provides the everyday class-level version of the same failure, but only through design-review evidence.

No field prevention claim is made. The Raymarine figures describe a bench prototype under a fixed scenario with eight participants. Schone Airspace Group provides design-representation checks, not flight performance, task completion time or operational error rates. Oceaneering provides design-review evidence, not measured dispatch behaviour.

No clinical or financial claim is made. Wrong-patient and wrong-account examples describe the failure category, not Creative Navy engagements on this page. No incident of any kind is claimed to have occurred or been averted.

## Related pages

This failure is closely related to Errors Are Easy To Make, because the two pages separate discrimination failures from binding failures. It also relates to Critical Actions Appear At The Wrong Time, Users Cannot See What State The System Is In and Errors Are Hard To Notice, because those pages cover neighbouring mechanisms: timing, system state and post-action detectability.

The Schone Airspace Group, Raymarine and Oceaneering case pages provide the engagement evidence behind this failure pattern. The Schone Airspace Group evidence is strongest for inspection-target separation. The Raymarine evidence is strongest for confirmation as a second decision point. The Oceaneering evidence shows the same mechanism when the selected object is a class rather than a single instance.
